artifact.canonical_name: OpenAI January agent-system engineering: Codex loop and in-house data agent

sources.title: Primary source 1: https://openai.com/index/inside-our-in-house-data-agent
sources.role: Primary source used for chronology and technical verification

sources.title: Primary source 2: https://openai.com/index/unrolling-the-codex-agent-loop
sources.role: Primary source used for chronology and technical verification

claims.text: OpenAI’s Codex article describes the agent loop as the harness logic orchestrating the user, model inference, tools, conversation history, and context-window management.

OpenAI’s in-house data-agent article describes an internal-only GPT-5.2 agent with layered context (metadata, human annotations, code enrichment, institutional knowledge, memory, runtime context) and pass-through access controls.
The data agent is explicitly an internal tool rather than a public product; examples of faster analysis and improved reliability are OpenAI-reported experience, not an independent benchmark.

limitations.text: The two sources describe different systems and should remain separately attributed even when used as one architecture cluster.
The in-house data-agent lessons are organizational case-study evidence and should not be generalized as a universal architecture benchmark.

artifact.canonical_name: Safe URL / agent link data-exfiltration safeguards

sources.title: Primary source 1: https://openai.com/index/ai-agent-link-safety
sources.role: Primary source used for chronology and technical verification

claims.text: OpenAI published a January 28 engineering note describing a URL-based data-exfiltration threat in which prompt-injected content can induce an agent to fetch a URL carrying conversation-derived secrets.

The described safeguard allows automatic retrieval for URLs independently observed as public and otherwise blocks the fetch or requires explicit user action; OpenAI presents this as one layer in a defense-in-depth strategy.

limitations.text: The mechanism targets URL-based exfiltration and does not establish that arbitrary web content is safe or that prompt injection is solved generally.
Security properties are implementation claims from OpenAI and are not independently penetration-tested here.

artifact.canonical_name: DynaWeb: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning of Web Agents

sources.title: Primary source 1: http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22149v2
sources.role: Primary source used for chronology and technical verification

claims.text: DynaWeb trains a web world model to predict page representations from agent actions, then uses it as a synthetic environment for model-based reinforcement learning rollouts.
The paper reports improvements on WebArena and WebVoyager for open-source web-agent models; these are author-reported experimental results.

limitations.text: A simulated web world model can differ materially from adversarial, dynamic live-web behavior.
The task locator is arXiv v2 updated after January; chronology should use the original January submission.

claims.text: vLLM v0.14.0 enabled async scheduling by default and added numerous engine, tool-calling, API, and model-support changes; the release notes explicitly call this a breaking change with unsupported configurations documented.
vLLM v0.15.0 added a Kimi-K2.5 architecture among new model support and extended async scheduling to pipeline parallelism, alongside streaming-input, quantization, and platform changes.
Any speedup figures in the release notes are project-reported and configuration dependent.

limitations.text: The series spans two releases nine days apart and should be summarized as serving/runtime evolution rather than one atomic feature.
Project performance claims are not independently reproduced.
